lesson.title: Inside the Machine: The Physical Parts That Make Computing Possible
lesson.summary: Introduces the major physical components of a computer, the CPU, memory, storage, and input and output devices, and how they connect to carry out the instructions described in earlier chapters.
lesson.body:
Every algorithm, function, and character code discussed so far in this course is, in the end, carried out by physical hardware: real electronic components that exist inside a case on a desk, inside a laptop, or inside a phone. Computer science studies computation as an abstract idea, but that idea only becomes useful once real machines can execute it. This section looks underneath the software layer, at the physical components that make running a Python program actually possible.

Most computers, from smartphones to supercomputers, are built around the same basic architecture, often credited to mathematician John von Neumann. In this design, a single memory space stores both the instructions of a program and the data that program works with, and a central processing unit reads and executes those instructions one at a time. This is why, when you run a Python script, both your code and the numbers or text it manipulates end up living in the same memory, at least while the program is running.

The central processing unit, or CPU, is the component that actually carries out instructions: performing arithmetic, comparing values, and deciding which instruction to run next. Memory, specifically random access memory or RAM, temporarily holds the instructions and data a running program currently needs, but RAM is volatile, meaning its contents disappear when power is lost. Secondary storage, such as a solid state drive or hard disk, holds data and programs permanently, even when the computer is turned off, but it is much slower to access than RAM, which is why running programs are loaded from storage into RAM first.

Rounding out the physical picture are input and output devices, often called I slash O devices, which let a computer exchange information with the outside world. A keyboard and mouse are input devices, sending information into the computer. A monitor and speakers are output devices, sending information back out. All of these components, the CPU, RAM, storage, and input and output devices, are connected by a set of electrical pathways called a bus, which carries data, memory addresses, and control signals between components so they can work together as a single system.

Understanding this hardware layer explains something that might otherwise seem mysterious: why programs can run slowly, why a computer can run out of memory, or why closing unused applications can speed things up. A Python program that stores an enormous list of numbers is really requesting a chunk of physical RAM, and if the computer's RAM is nearly full, the operating system may need to shuffle data between RAM and the much slower storage drive, which noticeably slows everything down. The next section looks even more closely at two of these components, the CPU and memory, and at exactly how they execute instructions.
